processing: As with other Yunnan raw pu-erh, the leaf is typically wilted, wok-fired, rolled and sun-dried into mao cha, then sold loose or steamed and pressed; no ripe-style pile fermentation.
harvest_season: Spring is the prized picking, as is usual for Mengku raw pu-erh; little is documented about the season here beyond that.
appearance_dry: Typical of Mengku large-leaf raw tea: long, thick dark green strands.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear golden yellow when young.
appearance_wet: Thick olive-green large leaves, as with other Mengku raw teas.
taste_profile: Little is documented about Bangdu's own taste. Mengku raw tea in general is sweet, fragrant and vigorous.

brewing.notes: General Mengku raw settings, since nothing specific to Bangdu is recorded.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year like other sheng: mostly as spring tea of a stated year, either as loose mao cha or pressed cakes. Young cakes of one to three years are the usual purchase, and those who store it age it for a decade or more. Ask for the year and the tree age, since old-tree and plantation leaf are priced far apart.
description:
Bangdu is one of the eight small areas on Mengku's eastern half-mountain, in the group known as the Mengku Eighteen Villages, alongside better-known Banuo and Nasai. The name is also written 帮读.

Nothing specific to Bangdu's processing is recorded, so assume the usual raw pu-erh method of the area. The local plant would typically be Mengku large-leaf, as is general in this district.

There is no solid tasting record of Bangdu by itself. Treat it as a Mengku raw tea and judge the actual sample: sweetness, how fast it turns bitter, and how many steeps it holds.

It should not be confused with Bangdong (邦东), a separate tea area elsewhere in Lincang. Check the characters on the wrapper when you buy.
history: Little is documented about Bangdu beyond its listing among the eastern half-mountain's small areas.
